databaselibraryreadingslab

“Immersion can be an intellectually stimulating process; however, in the present as in the past, in most cases immersion is mentally absorbing and a process, a change, a passage from one mental state to another. It is characterized by diminishing critical distance to what is shown and increasing emotional involvement in what is happening.”

Oliver Grau, Virtual Art: From Illusion to Immersion 13

the argument

1 a new medium with an old history

  • “this study shows clearly how, in each epoch, extraordinary efforts were made to produce maximum illusion with the technical means at hand” 5
  • “The panorama is also exemplary in that this effect was an intended one, a precalculated outcome of the application of technological, physiological, and psychological knowledge.” 6
  • “attention centers on 360° images, such as the frescoes, the panorama, circular cinema, and computer art in the CAVE: media that are the means whereby the eye is addressed with a totality of images” 5
  • “On the contrary, virtual reality forms part of the core of the relationship of humans to images.” 5
  • “In its concentration, the transmedia functional continuum of the hermetic illusion space appears to be an anthropological constant.” 340

immersion

2 the definition, and what it encloses

  • “Immersion can be an intellectually stimulating process; however, in the present as in the past, in most cases immersion is mentally absorbing and a process, a change, a passage from one mental state to another. It is characterized by diminishing critical distance to what is shown and increasing emotional involvement in what is happening.” 13
  • “these images integrate the observer in a 360° space of illusion, or immersion, with unity of time and place” 13
  • “Of the two main poles of meaning of the image, representative function and constitution of presence, it is the second that concerns this study.” 14
  • “Virtual realities—both past and present—are in essence immersive.” 15
  • “in Western art and media history there is a recurrent movement that seeks to blur, negate, or abolish this differentiation using the latest imaging techniques” 17

the arc

3 each epoch, its maximum illusion

illusion spacethe book's sentencep.
the Roman fresco“The most effective examples of these frescoes use motifs that address the observer from all sides in a unity of time and place, enclosing him or her hermetically.” 2525
the panorama“the worlds of illusion held for the public who, together with the images of war they experienced, also absorbed the ideology, submission, and obedience that were to lead them into the First World War.” 9696
the twentieth century“The desire to be in the picture, in both the metaphorical and nonmetaphorical sense, did not disappear with the panorama but lived on in the twentieth century.” 141141
the virtual environment“Many virtual environments reduce the observer to a disembodied state within a Cartesian space that is clear for miles around and often quite empty.” 193193

what the computer adds

4 the image as a space you enter

  • “In virtual reality, a panoramic view is joined by sensorimotor exploration of an image space that gives the impression of a “living” environment. Interactive media have changed our idea of the image into one of a multisensory interactive space of experience with a time frame.” 7
  • “The classic position of an observer directly in front of a material work of art was replaced by a participatory relationship that surmounts great distances but still appears to be immediately present in the work.” 271
  • “The Home of the Brain was an early glimpse of the epistemic innovation represented by telepresence, where in its reception the work loses its locatability.” 271

the interface decides

5 where reflection is possible, and where it is designed out

  • “A question that needs to be asked in this connection is whether there is still any place for distanced, critical reflection—a hallmark of the modern era—in illusion spaces experienced through interaction.” 10
  • “The fact that the computer program is visible does not detract substantially from the immersive experience; it reveals in part the binary foundations of the image spaces and, in this way, makes the observer aware of the origins of the illusion.” 196
  • “The more “natural” the interfaces become, the greater the danger—not only that most of the “technological iceberg” will be inaccessible to the user who is unaware of it—that there will be an illusionary disappearance of boundaries to the data space.” 203

what it costs

6 the medium disappears

  • “a constant characteristic of the principle of immersion is to conceal the appearance of the actual illusion medium by keeping it beneath the perceptive threshold of the observer to maximize the intensity of the messages that are being conveyed. The medium becomes invisible.” 340
  • “Immersion arises when artwork and technologically advanced apparatus, message and medium, are perceived to merge inseparably. In this moment of calculated “totalization,” the artwork is extinguished as an autonomously perceived aesthetic object for a limited period of time.” 339
  • “Immersive art often molds propagandistic messages, conveyed by its images, thus working specifically against distanced and critical reflection.” 339

7 power and the audience

  • “For, in essence, all socially relevant new image media, from classical antiquity to the revolution of digital images, have advanced to serve the interests of maintaining power and control or maximizing profits; hardly ever have they advanced solely for artistic purposes.” 339
  • “It is an apparent feature of the concept of immersion that it engages with the spatial and pictorial concentration of the awareness of one's own people, the formation of collective identity through powerful images that occupy the functions of memory.” 342
  • “The gain in power of suggestion is thus revealed as a primary goal and core motivation in the development of new media of illusion.” 342
  • “Within the tradition of illusionism, virtual image spaces should be understood as a vanishing point, as an extreme, where the relationship of humans to images is highlighted with particular clarity.” 341

8 the medium digital art depends on

  • “A further problem is that the longevity of digital art depends on its storage media. The permanent process of changing operating systems, for example, means that it is no longer possible to show some works that are not even ten years old.” 10

source: writings/Virtual Art - From Illusion to Immersion - Oliver Grau.pdf — Oliver Grau, Virtual Art: From Illusion to Immersion, translated by Gloria Custance, MIT Press, 2003. Page numbers are the book's own.
